facts.statement: Qiaowanlong fossils were discovered in the Yujinzi Basin of modern-day Gansu Province, China.
facts.quote: Fossils belonging to the genus were found in the Yujinzi Basin of what is today Gansu Province, China.

facts.statement: Qiaowanlong lived during the late Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: dating to the late Aptian Stage of the Early Cretaceous.

facts.statement: Qiaowanlong was formally described and named by Hai-Lu You and Da-Qing Li in 2009.
facts.quote: The description was finally published in 2009 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B by the Chinese scientists Hai-Lu You and Da-Qing Li.

facts.statement: The genus name Qiaowanlong refers to the nearby cultural site of Qiaowan, derived from the Chinese words for 'bridge' and 'bend in a stream'.
facts.quote: The name of the genus, Qiaowanlong is a reference to an important cultural site (Qiaowan) which is located near to where the fossils of Qiaowanlong were discovered.

facts.statement: The species name kangxii honors the Kangxi Emperor, who reportedly dreamed of the Qiaowan area.
facts.quote: The species epithet, Q. kangxii, is in honor of the Kangxi Emperor, who was said to have had dreams of the Qiaowan area.

facts.statement: The longest known vertebra of Qiaowanlong, the seventh cervical vertebra, measures 45 cm in length.
facts.quote: the seventh cervical vertebra (the longest of the known vertebrae) is 45 cm in length.

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul estimated Qiaowanlong to be about 12 meters long and weigh 6 tons.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul suggested a length of about 12 m long and a weight of 6 tons

facts.statement: Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi estimated Qiaowanlong to be 20.7 meters long, 4.3 meters tall at the shoulder, and 13 tons in weight.
facts.quote: Rubén Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi suggested a much larger estimate of 20.7 m long, 4.3 m tall at the shoulder, and 13 tons in weight.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Qiaowanlong consists of eight neck vertebrae, the right half of a pelvis, and unidentified bone fragments.
facts.quote: The holotype, and only specimen of Qiaowanlong consists of a series of eight vertebrae from the middle of the neck (probably C4-C11), the complete right half of the pelvis, and several bone fragments that the authors were not able to identify.

facts.statement: Later analyses placed Qiaowanlong within Euhelopodidae, suggesting a closer relationship to titanosaurs than to brachiosaurids.
facts.quote: Subsequent analyses have found a close relationship between Qiaowanlong and the other Asian sauropods Euhelopus and Erketu, which would place it within Euhelopodidae and therefore imply a closer affinity with titanosaurs than with brachiosaurids.

facts.statement: Qiaowanlong is classified within the unranked group Titanosauriformes.
Qiaowanlong lived approximately 100 million years ago during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous in what is now Asia.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 100 millones de años durante el Albiense, en lo que es hoy Asia.

facts.statement: The time range for Qiaowanlong is estimated between 121.4 and 113.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Aptian (121.4 to 113.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: During the Early Cretaceous, the habitat of Qiaowanlong was likely a less arid environment near the coast of the Tethys Sea.
facts.quote: Today, this region is part of the Gobi Desert, but during the Early Cretaceous, it was a much less arid environment, and it was probably on or near the coast of the Tethys Sea.

facts.statement: The environment of Qiaowanlong likely consisted of lowlands surrounded by narrow hills that allowed for easy movement of dinosaur populations.
facts.quote: The composition of the Xiagou Formation indicates that there were likely lowlands surrounded by narrow hills, allowing dinosaur faunas to travel across areas without geographical barriers.

facts.statement: Animals that may have coexisted with Qiaowanlong include the ornithopods Xuwulong and Jintasaurus, the tyrannosauroid Xiongguanlong, and the therizinosaur Suzhousaurus.
facts.quote: Other animals known from the Xiagou Formation, which may have directly coexisted with Qiaowanlong, included the ornithopods, Xuwulong and Jintasaurus, the tyrannosauroid, Xiongguanlong, and the therizinosaur, Suzhousaurus.

facts.statement: Qiaowanlong was initially reported as the first brachiosaurid found in China, but later analysis showed it is more closely related to titanosauriforms like Euhelopus and Erketu.
facts.quote: Qiaowanlong fue reportado inicialmente como el primer braquiosáurido encontrado en China. Sin embargo, un análisis posterior encontró que estaba más estrechamente relacionado con titanosauriformes como Euhelopus y Erketu.
